1) Answer

Yes. Across two decades, David Lammy has repeatedly taken positions and actions that prioritise equality, the rule of law and the protection of people’s rights at home and abroad. Representative evidence:

- Independent equality work in the justice system: He led the Lammy Review (2016–2017), an independent review for the UK government into racial disparities in the criminal justice system, making 35 recommendations centred on fairness, transparency and “explain or change.” The government formally responded and adopted key principles, indicating both the seriousness of the work and his sustained focus on rights-based reform. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/lammy-review-final-report?utm_source=openai))

- Defending citizenship and due process in the Windrush scandal: In 2018–2019 he used parliamentary tools (urgent questions) and public advocacy to press the government over unlawful detentions, deportations and denial of services to Windrush Britons, describing it as a “day of national shame.” This is concrete, sustained defence of individuals’ rights against state injustice. ([parliament.uk](https://www.parliament.uk/business/news/2018/april/urgent-question-windrush-scandal/?utm_source=openai))

- Advancing equal rights for LGBTQ+ people: In the Commons same‑sex marriage debates he argued explicitly that “separate but equal is a fraud,” and voted in favour of equal marriage—an archetypal human-rights position in UK lawmaking. The record is in Hansard. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2013-02-05/debates/13020551000002/Marriage%28SameSexCouples%29?utm_source=openai))

- Using foreign policy levers to uphold human rights and international humanitarian law (IHL) as Foreign Secretary (5 July 2024–5 Sept 2025): 
  - Suspended around 30 UK arms export licences to Israel after the government’s IHL assessment found a “clear risk” of misuse—an explicitly rights‑based application of export‑control law. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-suspends-around-30-arms-export-licences-to-israel-for-use-in-gaza-over-international-humanitarian-law-concerns?utm_source=openai))
  - Sanctioned individuals, illegal outposts and organisations linked to settler violence in the West Bank and paused UK‑Israel trade talks—framed as action against “heinous abuses of human rights.” ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-hit-west-bank-violence-network?utm_source=openai))
  - Formally recognised the State of Palestine as part of a framework aimed at equal rights, security and a two‑state peace—aligning UK policy with self‑determination and international law. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-formally-recognises-palestinian-state?utm_source=openai))
  - Drove multiple UK sanctions packages against Russia’s “shadow fleet” and other enablers of aggression, justifying them as measures to constrain abuses and uphold international law during the war in Ukraine. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-imposes-new-wave-of-sanctions-choking-russian-oil-revenues-with-foreign-secretary-arriving-in-italy-for-g7?utm_source=openai))
  - Announced a world‑first UK sanctions regime targeting organised people‑smuggling—framed as protecting vulnerable people from exploitation. ([questions-statements.parliament.uk](https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2025-01-09/hlws355?utm_source=openai))
  - Published a UK “Voluntary Report” on domestic implementation of IHL—stating a government commitment to compliance with humanitarian rules in conflict. ([questions-statements.parliament.uk](https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2024-10-16/hlws139?utm_source=openai))

- Current role: Since 5 September 2025 he has been Lord Chancellor, Justice Secretary and Deputy Prime Minister; the record above covers both his domestic rights work and, while Foreign Secretary, his rights‑oriented use of sanctions, export controls and diplomacy. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/people/david-lammy?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—independent equality work in the justice system, defence of due process and citizenship at home, votes and arguments for equal marriage, and a foreign policy that conditions exports and deploys sanctions around human‑rights and IHL concerns—the evidence shows Lammy values human rights in principle and in practice.
